Senses.Explanation: Cold and utterly still: in technical Chan use, the sensory chill becomes a compact description of motionless, stripped-down stillness. Shishuang Qingzhu’s formula places it among resting, one-thought-for-ten-thousand-years, and an old-shrine censer; Yuanwu Keqin then explains the body and mind as wood or stone. Guyan Bi’s self-praise binds it to dryness and lack of breath, while Hongzhi Zhenjue supplies the decisive limit: at the cold-still place one must become warm, just as dry ground needs moisture.

Senses.Explanation: Its recorded neighbors make the image concrete: “the cold furnace has no smoke; a bean pops in cold ashes” (寒爐煙絕，冷灰豆爆); a public question asks, “leaving aside a withered tree flowering, what about when a bean pops in cold ashes?” and receives “a thunderclap on level ground” (平地一聲雷). Other addresses follow the phrase with impossible growth—stone bamboo shoots sprout, flame comes from an icy river, an iron tree flowers, and a wooden man claps—or simply with “suddenly, one sound” (驀地一聲). The corpus also speaks of “a person in whom a bean has popped in cold ashes” (冷灰豆爆底人), making the image an appraisal in an interview. Zen bends a domestic image of an unlikely pop from spent ash into a stock address and interview phrase, repeatedly paired with sound and impossible renewal. Those pairings are the texts’ own; this entry assigns no hidden event to the image.

Senses.Explanation: Deshan's no-answer address is the public case in which Deshan announces that he will answer no questions that night and that any questioner receives thirty blows; when the monastic merely comes out and bows, Deshan strikes him and continues the encounter. Later masters use the compact case-name as a test and repeatedly set it against Zhaozhou's answer-required address, but their appraisals do not collapse into one verdict: Yuanwu Keqin calls it fastening locks and cangues, while Xiaoyin Daxin says its earlier move does not reach.

Deshan summons Yantou, who privately states his meaning; the next day's ascent of the seat differs from usual, and Yantou then celebrates Deshan's understanding. Mi'an answers 'what is its meaning?' with 'no meaning,' then says, 'if he wanted to go, he went; if he wanted to sit, he sat'; Xutang answers the same named case with 'buying dear and selling cheap.' These comments remain divergent responses to one inherited case.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1377.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Songyuan Chongyue. Returning after more than a month away from the community, Songyuan Chongyue recalls an older warning against a monk leaving the assembly. He admits that his own travels have brought mud and water with them, then asks how thick his face is. His answer is the inherited formula: the Yin used cypress, the Zhou chestnut. The tree names cap a self-question about his return rather than describe trees growing outside the monastery. The text does not explain precisely how the formula answers facial thickness; its abruptness and reference to differing earlier practices should remain visible instead of being replaced by an invented moral about either dynasty.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan. At the Buddha's final-release commemoration, Wuzhun Shifan raises the Buddha's final gesture and says a Chan practitioner does not even relish hearing the word 'Buddha,' much less examining his golden body. What, then, has extinction or non-extinction to do with him? Yet why will he shortly burn incense and bow in the main hall? He answers with the Yin's cypress and Zhou's chestnut. The headword caps the tension between refusing a fixed sacred image and participating in inherited ritual. It gestures toward differently established forms without spelling out a general rule that all practices are equivalent.

Its juxtaposition is the point the reader must confront, rather than a claim that either dynasty's custom supplies a final standard for Chan conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 剎微塵數教海、有阿僧祇佛剎微塵數眾生，皆入毘盧境界。大眾若見得、聞得，始知咳唾、掉臂、折旋、俯仰，時時與盧舍那如來磕頭撞額，步步不離華藏莊嚴世界海，可謂世界無盡，主伴重重，圓融行布，因果交徹，乃至成相、壞相，同相、異相，總相、別相，理法界、事法界，理事無礙法界、事事無礙法界，都在者拄杖頭上。所以道：剎塵心念可數知，大海中水可飲盡，虛空可量風可繫，無能盡說佛功德。」復卓拄杖，云：「大眾！者是拄杖子，且道盧舍那如來即今在甚麼處？」抴杖，下座。上堂。「月皎霜清鶴夢癡，一溪寒碧鎖煙絲，分明都是拈花旨，兩手而今付阿誰？須領略，莫狐疑，朔風劈面急如箭。」喝一喝，云：「穿過髑髏幾箇知？」臘八，解制，上堂。「黃龍有三關，青龍只一關。」拈拂子畫一。「於此透得，許諸人與釋迦老子同行、同坐、同修、同證、同成正覺，任你烈烈轟轟、吒吒沙沙，鍼鋒上走馬、芥子內藏山，然者些伎倆到衲僧門下大似糞艸堆頭一敝屣耳。須知更有向上一著子在，且道是那一著？」揮拂，云：「殷勤為解丁香結，放出枝頭自在春。」誕日，請上堂。「慚愧今朝母難日，多年祖道無成立。街頭拾得一明珠，接物利生用不訖。無隱匿，天上人間稱第一。」上堂。「雨過垂楊淡鎖，煙流水夕陽邊。生涯豐儉且隨緣，饑餐與倦眠。佛懶做，說甚仙？風光滿目前。鐵笛橫吹雲外，天明月下晴川。」上堂。「俯仰折旋，不離菩提覺場；語默施為，總是般若玅用。翠竹恒露法身，黃花全彰祖意。絡緯籬邊，夜織無絲之絹；蟾蜍天際，常轉不退之輪。石女挑蜀錦，不藉功勳；木童唱吳歌，渾超音律。非見聞之可到，豈意解之能通？天然尊貴，迥出常情。大眾還會麼？禮之用，和為貴，先王之道斯為美。」至獅子林，請上堂。「目前無法，意在目前，不是目前法，非耳目之所到。夾山大似拈一放一。怎如青龍渡練州涉羅溪。昨在臥石菴中，今到獅子林裏。沿途而來，只見白雲澹泞、秋水澂渟，蘆花與明月交輝、丹楓共落霞爭錦，木樨香透山谷鼻孔、芙蓉笑破迦葉容顏。若是箇漢，正好騎聲蓋色，罩古籠今，傾湫倒嶽，雨施雲興。直下似箇獅子兒，吒沙哮吼一聲，野獸潛跡、飛禽亂墜。正恁麼時，直饒佛祖，不敢近傍，更有何物而能當情？且道誰是其人？」畫○：「昨夜三更月到窗。」至萬善菴，請上堂。「向上一著，千聖茫然，貴乎當人眼疾手快，掠得便行，乃可斥雷逐電，撼蕩乾坤，驅耕夫之牛、奪饑

Senses.Explanation: The records use this transitive appraisal for seeing through a saying, case, person, condition, or position before or after it is presented. Literally, 'look through' or 'look and break through.' The compound is attested. It is used transitively of a saying, case, person, condition, or distinction; in passive clauses someone or something is 'seen through.' Hongzhi asks, 'What is the eye with which you can see through it?'. Comments on earlier cases say that someone saw through Lingyun and Mahakasyapa, that Tianning saw through Dahui, or that an interlocutor should see through an action before it occurs. The passive form appears in a warning about being seen through by someone at a later time (他時異日被人覷破). The fuller form 'be able to see through' is attested, while the emphatic 'with one look, see through' (一覷覷破) is attested. The texts do not supply a separate technical definition beyond these observable objects, contrasts, questions, and active/passive constructions.

Senses.Note: Buying straw sandals and travelling further is a pointed reply to premature completion. Senses.Note: In the Danxia wooden-Buddha case, Ying'an Tanhua refuses to treat the steward's fallen eyebrows as simple loss: the steward has bought iron and found gold. Yinyuan uses the phrase for an unexpectedly rich glimpse of one's own footing, but warns against careless acceptance. Huqiu says Zifu gained in this way when he drew a circle for a visitor, then says the case remains unfinished. Chaozong quotes Ying'an and Gao-feng's opposing comments and asks whether either has understood the steward's eyebrows. The gain is real enough to challenge an easy verdict of failure, yet it does not close the case.

Senses.Explanation: Ying'an says the steward who loses his eyebrows after Danxia burns a wooden Buddha has bought iron and received gold. Yinyuan voices the saying as a warning that a glimpse may bring unexpected gain; Huqiu applies it to Zifu's drawn circle. Chaozong quotes Ying'an's verdict and then tests whether either of two older teachers settled the Danxia case.
